Talk
tawk
v.i. and n. (familiar speech, conversation; rendering Hebrew dabar, siach, Greek laleo, homileo)
Middle English talken, a frequentative of tell. Scripture treats ordinary conversation with a seriousness the word's casualness disguises — it is the medium of household discipleship, and it is entered as evidence at the judgment.

Biblical Definition

Talk is ordinary conversation, and Scripture assigns it two roles: it is the chief instrument of raising children in the faith, and it is evidence at the last day. The Shema's instruction to Israel places doctrine in the flow of household life rather than in a classroom: “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Four settings, covering the whole day, none of them formal. The Lord Jesus then puts unconsidered speech into the record: “every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36) — idle meaning unemployed, thrown off, the words a man would not defend and does not remember. Paul gives the positive rule with an economy that leaves no room for the usual exemptions: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers” (Ephesians 4:29). The test is not whether speech is true but whether it builds and whether it gives grace to those who hear. And Job's friend Zophar, wrong about much, is right about this: “should a man full of talk be justified?” (Job 11:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Ordinary conversation, and Scripture takes it seriously. Deuteronomy makes talk the medium of household discipleship across the whole day; Christ says idle words are accounted for; Paul requires speech that edifies and ministers grace to hearers.

expand to see more

TALK, v.i. tauk. To converse familiarly; to speak, as in familiar discourse, when two or more persons interchange thoughts.

2. To prate; to speak impertinently.

3. To talk of, to relate; to tell; to give an account of.

TALK, n. Familiar converse; mutual discourse; that which is uttered by one person in familiar conversation.

5. Subject of discourse; as, this is the talk of the town. Shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house. Deut. 6.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 6:7 — "And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

Matthew 12:36 — "But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment."

Ephesians 4:29 — "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers."

Job 11:2 — "Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified?"

Modern Corruption

Speech has been reclassified as harmless in itself — talk is just talk, and only actions count — at the same time that a rival error treats certain words as harmful in a nearly magical sense, with both readings missing what Scripture actually weighs.

expand to see more

The first assumption is the folk wisdom that words are cheap and deeds are what matter. Scripture treats speech as a principal work, not a substitute for one. The tongue is a fire and a world of iniquity, defiling the whole body (James 3:6); by thy words thou shalt be justified and by thy words condemned (Matthew 12:37); death and life are in the power of the tongue (Proverbs 18:21). Christ's reason in Matthew 12 is diagnostic: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh, so unguarded talk is the most reliable available sample of the inner man — which is precisely why the idle word, not the prepared statement, is the one entered in evidence. A church that disciplines for adultery and tolerates a slanderous tongue for thirty years has not read the epistles it preaches from.

The opposite error inflates certain words into contaminants whose mere utterance injures, and it usually arrives with a list. Scripture's categories are different and more searching. Ephesians 4:29 does not supply a vocabulary of forbidden terms; it applies a functional test — does this build up, and does it give grace to the hearers? — which condemns a great deal of perfectly polite speech: the accurate report that damages, the joke at a brother's expense, the theological correction delivered to wound. And Deuteronomy 6:7 supplies the positive charge that most households neglect. Faith is transmitted mainly through unscheduled talk — sitting, walking, lying down, rising up — which means a father who outsources his children's instruction entirely to a Sunday programme has not delegated the duty but declined it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar (to speak) and siach (to muse, converse); Greek laleo (to speak, utter), homileo (to converse — the root of homily), and logos (word, account).

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1696) — to speak, talk; the verb in Deuteronomy 6:7 and the root of dabar, a word or thing.

Hebrew siach (H7878) — to muse, meditate, talk; the verb in Psalm 119:15 and 1 Chronicles 16:9.

Greek laleo (G2980) — to speak, utter; the ordinary verb of speech, distinct from lego, to say with content.

Greek homileo (G3656) — to converse, talk with; used of the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:14-15).

Greek argos (G692) — idle, unemployed, unproductive; the adjective in Matthew 12:36, the same word rendered barren in 2 Peter 1:8.

Usage

"“Shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house” — four settings covering the whole day, none of them formal."

"“Every idle word… they shall give account” — the unguarded word is the most reliable sample of the heart."

"“That it may minister grace unto the hearers” — the test is not truth alone but whether it builds."
